Team Name: STEAMTroopers 24
Team #: 18000
Challenge Division: Elementary
Challenge Identifier: Plant the Moon
Location: Lowpoint-Washburn Middle School, Washburn, IL USA
Team Members: AJ Whirrell, Ryder Baugh, Liam Seibert,
Konner Kennell, Zane Womack, Zander Aeschleman
How Will Different Types of Natural Fertilizer Affect Soybeans Grown in Lunar Regolith and Illinois
Black Soil?
Background: Last spring, some of our team members competed in the Plant the Moon Challenge and grew
soybeans in different ratios of lunar regolith and Illinois black soil. We decided to test soybeans again this year.
Before setting up our experiment, we talked to a few local farmers to help us better understand soybean
growth. We came up with the idea of testing what would happen if we added natural fertilizer to the 70% lunar
regolith/30 % Illinois black soil ratio. Soybeans: Illinois is the top producer of soybeans in the United States.
Our school is in a rural area and we are surrounded by soybean fields. Soybeans are high in fiber and protein
and low in saturated fats.They are also cholesterol and lactose free. They are a good source of omega-3 fatty
acids and antioxidants. When a soybean first sprouts, you see the cotyledons. That’s where the food for the
new plant is held. Sometimes one of the cotyledons falls off. The soybean can still continue to grow with just
one. When you grow soybeans, you can save some of the soybeans to start new plants. Illinois Black Soil:
Our state is well-known for its rich soil. It is very black in color. Most of the soil around us is Drummer soil. It is
known to produce the highest yields of soybeans. Lunar Regolith: According to NASA at nasa.gov, regolith on
the moon is made up of chips of rocks, small pieces of mineral, volcanic glass, and a substance called
agglutinates. Agglutinates can only be found on the moon and are made when tiny, tiny pieces of minerals are
melted together with a little bit of soil when hit by a micrometeorite.One big difference between our lunar
regolith and our Illinois black soil is that the lunar regolith does not contain organic matter. Natural Fertilizers:
We chose to test fresh chicken, cow, hog, and sheep manure. Chicken Manure: Chicken manure adds a slow
release of macro and micronutrients. It adds nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium to the soil, more than cow
manure. It also helps to hold the moisture in the soil. Cow Manure: Cow manure also adds nitrogen,
phosphorus, and potassium, but also adds sulfur and magnesium. Hog Manure: Hog manure adds nitrogen,
potassium, and phosphorus to plants and helps to hold moisture in the soil. Sheep Manure: Sheep manure is
high in potassium and phosphorus which help plants establish strong roots and fight pests.
Project Hypothesis or Aim: The STEAMTroopers 24 Plant the Moon Team predicted that if we planted one
soybean seed in a mixture of 280 grams of lunar regolith mixed with 120 grams of good Illinois black soil and
added four different types of natural fertilizer (chicken, cow, hog, and sheep manure), the soybeans planted
with hog manure would grow the best. We thought the hog manure would work best because when we
researched we read that hog manure helps to hold moisture in soil. From our experiment last year, we knew
that the lunar regolith can get really dry so we thought the hog manure would help hold the moisture in the
regolith. We also thought that the hog manure would help add the needed nutrients that the lunar regolith is
missing, especially nitrogen.
Independent Variables: The independent variables or the variable that changed in our experiment were the
different types of natural fertilizer. So our independent variables were cow, sheep, hog and chicken manure.
We tested two pots with each manure.

Dependent Variables: The dependent variables or what we were measuring in our experiment were the height
of the soybeans and the number of leaves that grew on each plant. We measured the height of the soybeans in
centimeters and then counted the leaves that grew on the plats and recorded that also.
Controls: We used Identical 4” pots, each with 280g of lunar regolith, 120g of Illinois black soil. Each pot was
planted with one soybean seed-all from the same package.The same grow lights for the same amount of time
(12 hours on and 12 hours off).. All pots were located in the same location. We watered all plants at the same
time. Watering was based on the plants’ moisture levels. Pot moisture levels 0-3 received 10 ml of water. Pot
moisture levels 4-6 received 5 ml of water, and if moisture levels were 7 or above no water was added. All pots
will grow for 8 weeks and data was recorded for 8 weeks. Two pots did not have any fertilizer added so they
could be our control pots.
Experimental Design and Procedures: To test if soybeans will grow best when mixed with 70% lunar
regolith/30% black soil and our 4 chosen manure fertilizers- chicken, cow, hog & sheep, we followed these
procedures:
1.
Mix 70% lunar regolith (280g) with 30% Illinois black soil (120g)
2.
Fill each pot with the 400g of lunar regolith/soil mixture.
3.
Measure out equal amount of manure (4g) for each pot
4.
Add chicken manure to pots 1A and 1B
5.
Add cow manure to pots 2A and 2B
6.
Add hog manure to pots 3A and 3B
7.
Add sheep manure to pots 4A and 4B
8.
Fill pots 5A and 5B with the mixture of 280 grams of lunar regolith and 120 grams of Illinois black soil.
We did not add any fertilizer. These pots were used as our control.
9.
Plant 1 soybean seed 10mm deep in each pot
10. We planned to water with 10mL of water each day. After the first week,
11. we noticed that several pots were testing too wet so we changed our
12. watering method to watering based on our moisture tests. If it was
13. between 0-3 we gave the pot 10mL, 4-6 got 5mL,
14. & anything over 6 did not get watered that day.
15. Set grow lights to be on 12 hours a day and off 12 hours a day
16. Record moisture level, growth, and leaf count each day.
Conclusion: In conclusion, after collecting growth data for eight weeks and analyzing it, we have concluded
that the soybeans planted in 280 grams of lunar regolith and 120 grams of Illinois black soil grew best when
sheep manure was added to the growth pots. Both of our sheep pots (Pots 4A and 4B) sprouted and grew the
tallest. They reached heights of 25 cm and 37 cm, for an average of 31 cm. After 4 weeks of growth, Pot 4B
reached 32 cm. We had to stake it to help support the stem. We would unwrap the stem to measure it. On
March 9th the stem broke off at 25 cm during the measuring. We were so sad to have lost our tallest plant, but
we kept watering it and were very surprised when new growth started coming out of the cotyledon. We
continued to measure the stem at 25 cm and used that for our final measurement, but would also like to report
that the new growth area has reached 18 cm. (See photo A). That plant also has the second most leaves and
remains a healthy plant. The cow manure pots and our control pots of just regolith and soil (no fertilizer)
resulted in only one plant growing. The seed sprouted in all pots but did not grow, the sprout died. The hog
manure pots had trouble getting started. We found that these pots, along with the chicken pots, held more
moisture than most of the other pots. We believe that the moisture delayed the sprouting of the hog manure
seeds. We did not have to water these pots as often. The chicken seeds would sprout but would not grow. We
replanted and had the same results the second planting. In total we have six healthy plants growing out of a

total of ten pots. They range in height from 21.5 cm to 37.5 cm. From our experiment, we would conclude that
a soybean seed planted in 280g of lunar regolith, 120g of Illinois black soil, and fertilized with sheep manure
will result with the best plant growth and leaf count. Both of the sheep plants are healthy and we really hope
they will eventually result in producing pods. Our conclusion does not match our hypothesis. We thought the
hog manure’s ability to keep soil moist would help the lunar regolith, but it seemed to keep too much moisture
and the seeds struggled.
Additional Comments: One of our most surprising discoveries was that the breaking of the stem resulted in
new growth lower on the stem coming from the cotyledon. We also learned that unwrapping the stem to measure
growth weakened the stem. To overcome this, we used string to wrap with the stem and then would measure the
string for a more accurate measurement of growth.(Photo B) We did have another incident to overcome. On the
afternoon of our planting, we were using electronic scales to measure our lunar regolith and Illinois black soil.
Suddenly, the room went dark, we had lost power. Then our phones sounded a warning and our principal
announced that there was a tornado spotted approximately 15-20 miles from the school. We all took shelter.
Luckily, we can report that it did not come our direction and the area that it touched down in only had minimal
damage and everyone was safe. However, our last pot (5B - one of our control pots) was not planted until the
next morning. We practiced safety first and will never forget how our Planting the Moon experience was
interrupted by Mother Nature.
